title: Telling time and daily routines
goal: Tell the time correctly, describe your daily routine — and get comfortable with how Portuguese counts the half hour: *sete e meia* is **half past seven**, never half to.
bekal: ask and tell the time, including half and quarter hours
use reflexive verbs (*acordar*, *levantar-se*, *deitar-se*) to describe your routine
avoid the "half" trap that flips the meaning

dialogs.title: Dialogue — A rotina de um dia comum
dialogs.intro: Carla and Budi are waiting for the bus. The conversation turns to their daily schedules.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.id: What time do you wake up?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Acordo às seis da manhã, todo dia.
lines.id: I wake up at six in the morning, every day.
lines.literal: I-wake-up at-the six of-the morning, every day.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Tão cedo! Eu acordo às nove.
lines.id: So early! I wake up at nine.
lines.literal: so early! I I-wake-up at-the nine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E a aula começa às dez, né?
lines.id: And class starts at ten, right?
lines.literal: and the class it-starts at-the ten, isn't-it?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Começa. Termina ao meio-dia e meia.
lines.id: Yes. It ends at half past twelve.
lines.literal: it-starts. it-ends at-the mid-day and half.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Depois eu almoço e trabalho até as sete e meia.
lines.id: Then I have lunch and work until half past seven.
lines.literal: after I I-lunch and I-work until the seven and half.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Nossa, que dia cheio! A que horas você janta?
lines.id: Gosh, what a full day! What time do you have dinner?
lines.literal: gosh, what day full! at what hours you you-dine?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Por volta das oito. Depois eu descanso.
lines.literal: by turn of-the eight. after I I-rest.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.id: And do you go to bed early?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I go to sleep at midnight. Never before.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Então você dorme só seis horas!
lines.id: So you only sleep six hours!
lines.literal: then you you-sleep only six hours!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pois é. Por isso eu estou sempre cansado.
lines.id: Yep. That's why I'm always tired.
lines.literal: so is. for that I I-am(estar) always tired.

notes: ⚠️ **The big trap of this unit: *meia* always counts forward.** Portuguese counts **forward** from the hour that has passed: *sete e meia* = "seven and a half" = **7:30**, like English *half past seven* (or British *half seven*). If you know German or Dutch, be careful: there "half eight" means 7:30. In Portuguese, *oito e meia* is always 8:30 — get it wrong and you'll arrive an hour early or late.

**Né?** is the most typically Brazilian word in this whole course. It's short for *não é?* and means "right?" — used at the end of a sentence to ask for agreement, just like English *right?* or *isn't it?*. If you take only one habit from this unit, take this one.

**Pois é** is an almost untranslatable expression. Literally "so it is", it means something like "yep, that's how it is" or "what can you do". Brazilians use it to agree with something slightly sad or that can't be changed.
**Por volta das oito** = "around eight". Note *das* — *de* + *as*, because *horas* is feminine plural. A more casual way: *lá pelas oito*.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The question is always *Que horas são?* and the answer uses *ser* — in the **plural**, because there are many hours.
after: ⚠️ **Only one o'clock uses *é*.** Every other hour uses *são*, because grammatically they're plural. Likewise *é meio-dia* and *é meia-noite* — both singular.
**Duas horas, not dois horas.** *Hora* is feminine, so the number two changes too. A direct application of the rule from unit 4, and it comes up every time you say two o'clock.

**In daily life, Brazilians use the 24-hour clock for official things** (bus timetables, movies, doctor's appointments): *o filme é às dezenove e trinta*. But in conversation they go back to the 12-hour clock and add *da manhã*, *da tarde*, *da noite*.

grammars.title: Reflexive verbs: the morning routine
body: Some verbs need a little pronoun because the subject does something **to themselves**. English sometimes says *myself* (*I get myself ready*), but usually leaves it out — Portuguese never does with these verbs.
after: **In Brazil, the little pronoun goes before the verb** — *eu me levanto*, not *eu levanto-me*. The second form is correct in Portugal and sounds very stiff in Brazil. Once again, this course uses the Brazilian form.
There are only three forms you need: **me** (myself), **se** (yourself, himself, herself, themselves), **nos** (ourselves). Since *você* and *ele* share a form, you really only learn two.

grammars.title: Routine verbs
body: Some of these are irregular. The "I" forms that break the pattern are marked.
after: **Tomar banho literally means "to take bath"**, and it's the only way to say "to shower" in Brazil. And *tomar café* means both "to have breakfast" and "to drink coffee" — context tells them apart.
⚠️ *Sair* means "to go out" and also "to go out and have fun": *Vamos sair hoje?* = "Want to go out tonight?". Its "I" form breaks the pattern: *saio* (said SY-oo).

English

blocks.text: ⚠️ Watch the pair *de manhã* and *da manhã*. The first stands alone (*Eu estudo de manhã* = I study in the morning); the second attaches to a time (*às seis da manhã* = at six in the morning). One of the most common small mistakes, and the easiest to avoid once you've noticed it.
To make plans, these two sentences are enough: *A que horas a gente se encontra?* ("What time shall we meet?") and *Pode ser às três?* ("Does three work?").

blocks.text: The best exercise for this unit: rewrite that table with your own times and activities. Ten sentences about your own life stick far better than a hundred about someone else's.

items: Where's the restroom? → *Onde fica o banheiro?*
The bank is next to the bakery → *O banco fica ao lado da padaria*
I live near the subway → *Eu moro perto do metrô*
The key is on the table → *A chave está em cima da mesa*
Turn right at the corner → *Vira à direita na esquina*
